anchor: How changed is here each spot
title: 'Thyrsis': occasion and genre
short: A pastoral elegy for Arthur Hugh Clough (1819-1861), who died in Florence; first printed in Macmillan's Magazine, April 1866, and collected in New Poems (1867).
body: Arnold subtitled the poem 'A Monody, to commemorate the author's friend, Arthur Hugh Clough, who died at Florence, 1861'. Clough died on 13 November 1861. The poem returns to the Cumnor hills near Oxford, the landscape of Arnold's 'The Scholar-Gipsy' (1853), and walks there on a winter evening. It belongs to the line of pastoral elegy from Theocritus and Bion through Milton's 'Lycidas' and Shelley's 'Adonais'. Critics have often noted how little of Clough the man appears in the poem, and still debate how far it mourns Clough and how far Arnold's own lost youth and poetic gift.

anchor: Are ye too changed, ye hills?
title: The stanza
short: Twenty-four ten-line stanzas, the same as 'The Scholar-Gipsy': pentameters with a short trimeter sixth line, rhymed abcbcadeed.
body: Arnold reuses the stanza of 'The Scholar-Gipsy', itself adapted from the stanza of Keats's odes. The ten lines are iambic pentameter except the sixth, a short line of three stresses ('Are ye too changed, ye hills?'). The short line acts as a hinge or sigh in mid-stanza. The rhymes interlace (fills / same / lacks / name / stacks / hills; men / strays / days / then). The return of the same stanza ties 'Thyrsis' to the earlier poem: it is literally a revisiting.

title: the two Hinkseys and Sibylla
short: North and South Hinksey, villages below Boars Hill west of Oxford; 'Sibylla' was a name on an inn sign, now gone.
body: The walk starts from Oxford over the Hinkseys toward Cumnor. The details of change are exact and local: a 'haunted mansion' gone from the village street, twisted chimney-stacks gone, and a woman's name gone from an inn sign. Sibylla was evidently the name of the inn's keeper, painted on its sign. The opening line sets the poem's argument: what man 'makes or fills' changes, so the question 'Are ye too changed, ye hills?' asks whether nature too has failed. The poet's return is only to find loss.

title: Childsworth Farm, Ilsley Downs, the Vale
short: Chilswell Farm on Boars Hill; from the ridge one sees the Ilsley Downs, the Vale of the White Horse, and the upper Thames.
body: 'Childsworth' is Arnold's form of Chilswell Farm, near the top of Boars Hill. From the ridge the view runs southwest to the Berkshire Downs around East Ilsley and over the Vale of the White Horse. The 'three lone weirs' and 'youthful Thames' are on the upper Thames near Oxford, 'youthful' in contrast to the broad lower river. The exact topography is part of the elegy's method: the friends' shared knowledge of every field and path becomes a form of memory.

title: 'that sweet city with her dreaming spires'
short: Oxford seen from the hills: Arnold's phrase became the city's lasting epithet.
body: The phrase made Oxford 'the city of dreaming spires'. Seen from the winter hills, the towers rise from the mist of the Thames valley. 'Dreaming' gives the city the meditative, half-asleep life of a place of study, and links it with the poem's language of reverie. Arnold elsewhere (preface to Essays in Criticism, 1865) praised Oxford as 'whispering from her towers the last enchantments of the Middle Age'. The next lines insist that she is lovely even in winter: 'She needs not June for beauty's heightening'.

title: the signal-elm
short: The lone tree on the ridge that the friends treated as a token: while it stood, the Gipsy-Scholar lived. Its identity (elm or oak) is debated.
body: Arnold makes the single tree a sacred sign of their youth. 'While it stood, we said, / Our friend, the Gipsy-Scholar, was not dead' (st. 3). At first he cannot see it and fears it is gone. Its rediscovery, 'Bare on its lonely ridge, the Tree! the Tree!' (st. 16), is the poem's turning point. Local tradition pointed to a tree near Chilswell; one later caption says the dead tree shown as its remains was in fact an oak. Philip J. Stewart (1981) used weather records, maps and evidence of tree growth to tie the tree to an experience of Arnold's in November 1863. The tree is the elegy's version of the traditional pastoral token.

title: the Gipsy-Scholar
short: The hero of Arnold's 'The Scholar-Gipsy' (1853), from Glanvill's story of a poor Oxford student who joined the gipsies to learn their secret lore.
body: Joseph Glanvill's The Vanity of Dogmatizing (1661) tells of an Oxford scholar who left the university for poverty and joined a band of gipsies to learn their arts, intending to give the world an account when he had mastered them. Arnold's 1853 poem made him an immortal wanderer haunting these same hills, seeking a light beyond modern 'sick hurry'. 'Thyrsis' calls him 'our friend' and closes with him: 'Our Scholar travels yet the loved hill-side'. The two poems are companions, written in the same stanza.

title: shepherd-pipes and the lost pipe
short: Pastoral code for writing poetry: here the friends first tried verse; Arnold's 'pipe is lost', since he had written little new poetry in recent years.
body: In pastoral elegy the poets are shepherds and their songs are played on pipes. 'Assay'd' means tried. Arnold's lament 'My pipe is lost, my shepherd's holiday!' refers to his own career. He had become a school inspector (from 1851) and Oxford Professor of Poetry (1857-67), and was turning increasingly to criticism. Having lost the pipe 'needs must' (of necessity), he went 'into the world and wave of men'. The contrast follows: 'But Thyrsis of his own will went away'.

anchor: of his own will went away
title: 'of his own will went away'
short: Clough left Oxford by choice, resigning his Oriel fellowship in 1848 over religious doubts about subscribing to the Thirty-Nine Articles.
body: Fellows had to subscribe to the Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles. Clough, troubled by religious doubt, resigned his fellowship and tutorship at Oriel College in 1848; he later became principal of University Hall, London (1849). Stanza 5 makes this a pastoral restlessness: 'It irk'd him to be here, he could not rest'. A 'shadow lour'd' (darkened) on the fields. 'Some life of men unblest / He knew' is Clough's sense of social suffering and religious unrest. 'Silly sheep' keeps the old sense of 'silly': innocent, helpless (compare Milton's 'silly thoughts' in the Nativity Ode).

title: the cuckoo's parting cry
short: Clough is like the cuckoo that leaves at the end of the first bloom of early summer; but the cuckoo returns next spring, and Thyrsis will not.
body: Cuckoos fall silent and leave in midsummer. Arnold hears the 'parting cry' as if the bird were saying 'The bloom is gone, and with the bloom go I!' He chides it as a 'Too quick despairer' and lists the high summer flowers it will miss (carnations, snapdragon, sweet-william, stocks, roses, jasmine). The contrast then turns: the bird 'next year ... will return'. That turn draws on the Lament for Bion, where mallows and garden herbs revive each year but men sleep 'a long, endless, unawakening sleep'.

title: Thyrsis and Corydon
short: In Virgil's seventh Eclogue the shepherd Thyrsis loses a singing match to Corydon; Arnold (Corydon) says Thyrsis has been beaten by Time instead.
body: Virgil's Eclogue 7 ends with the judge's verdict: 'I remember how Thyrsis was beaten and strove in vain; from then on Corydon has been Corydon for us' (7.69-70). Arnold adopts the names, himself as Corydon and Clough as Thyrsis. The two names come ultimately from Theocritus (Thyrsis sings the lament for Daphnis in Idyll 1). The line courteously reverses the contest: Clough's death was not defeat by a rival poet but by Time. The next stanza laments 'for Corydon no rival now'.

anchor: when Sicilian shepherds lost a mate
title: the Sicilian shepherds and Bion
short: From the Lament for Bion: the Sicilian elegist imagines going down to Pluto, like Orpheus, to sing for his dead friend and win him back.
body: Sicily was the home of pastoral (Theocritus, and traditionally Bion and Moschus). The Lament for Bion, formerly attributed to Moschus, imagines its poet going down to Pluto and singing to Persephone, who as a Sicilian girl would know the Dorian songs and let Bion return. The 'unpermitted ferry' is Charon's boat over the Styx, which living men may not cross. Arnold follows this closely, with 'flute his friend, like Orpheus, from the dead': Orpheus's music won Eurydice back from Hades. Arnold's turn in the next stanza is that this hope fails in the Thames valley.

anchor: Of Proserpine, among whose crowned hair
title: Proserpine and Enna
short: Proserpine was carried off by Pluto while gathering flowers at Enna in Sicily; Arnold echoes Milton's account in Paradise Lost.
body: Ovid tells how Pluto (Dis) seized Proserpina as she picked violets and lilies near Enna in Sicily (Metamorphoses 5.385-424). Milton's Paradise Lost 4.268-72 speaks of 'that fair field / Of Enna, where Proserpin gathering flowers / Herself a fairer flower by gloomy Dis / Was gathered'. Arnold's 'lily white which Enna yields' and 'flowers first open'd on Sicilian air' draw on this tradition. Because she was herself Sicilian, the Dorian shepherds' songs reached her easily ('O easy access to the hearer's grace').

anchor: the Dorian pipe, the Dorian strain
title: Dorian
short: Many Greek settlers of Sicily were Dorians, so the pastoral of Theocritus is written in a literary Doric dialect; 'Dorian' here means Sicilian pastoral.
body: Syracuse and other Sicilian cities were founded largely by Dorian Greeks (Syracuse from Corinth). Theocritus's bucolic poems use a Doric literary dialect, and 'Doric' became a byword for pastoral simplicity. Milton's 'Lycidas' ends with the swain singing his 'Doric lay'. The insistent repetition (Dorian shepherds, Dorian water, Dorian pipe, Dorian strain) builds the classical world that is lost in the next lines: 'But ah, of our poor Thames she never heard!'

title: Cumner, Fyfield, Ensham, Sandford
short: Cumnor (Arnold's 'Cumner') and its hills, the Fyfield elm, and the Thames villages of Eynsham ('Ensham') and Sandford, above and below Oxford.
body: The English place-names answer the Sicilian ones. Cumnor lies west of Oxford on the hills of the poem. Fyfield, further west, had a famous elm also mentioned in 'The Scholar-Gipsy'. Eynsham and Sandford lie up- and down-stream of Oxford, so 'Above ... down' measures the whole river. Arnold's spelling 'Ensham' follows older usage. The famous fritillaries (snake's-head lilies, white and purple) grow in the Thames water-meadows. The catalogue asserts the poet's local knowledge: 'Who, if not I, for questing here hath power?'

title: the Wytham flats and the girl at the boatman's door
short: The flat meadows by the Thames at Wytham, northwest of Oxford; the memory of a boatman's girl and mowers recalls the Scholar-Gipsy's river scenes.
body: Wytham's meadows lie along the Thames upstream of Oxford. The stanza remembers rowing past red loosestrife and meadow-sweet, the girl who untied their skiff, and the mowers who stopped 'with suspended scythe to see us pass'. It is ubi sunt: 'Where is ... ? Where are ... ?', the classical and medieval lament form asking where the past has gone. The answer comes flatly: 'They all are gone, and thou art gone as well!'

anchor: the brown hair sprent with grey
title: night and age, 'sprent with grey'
short: Night, personified, closes round the poet: grief for Clough turns into awareness of his own ageing. 'Sprent' = sprinkled, flecked.
body: 'Sprent' is the old past participle of 'sprenge', to sprinkle; the OED records it as archaic. Night weaves her shade 'in ever-nearing circle' and lays her 'finger light / ... pausefully upon life's headlong train'. The list of symptoms is personal: less eager feet, less bounding heart, hope 'less quick to spring again'. Arnold was 43 in 1866. Stanza 15 turns the mood philosophical: the 'throne of Truth' on the mountain-tops seems further, the world's fort 'unbreachable', and death 'as welcome as a friend'.

title: the mountain-tops and the throne of Truth
short: In youth the summits of truth looked near and bright; in middle age the way looks long, and the world's walls look impregnable.
body: The landscape becomes allegory. 'Sanguine youth' (hopeful, from the sanguine humour) misjudged distances. The 'fort / Of the long-batter'd world', besieged by reformers, will not fall. This reflects the shared hopes of Arnold and Clough in the 1840s, the revolutionary year of 1848 and its aftermath. The temptation here, to welcome death as rest, is answered by the omen of the tree.

title: 'Bare on its lonely ridge, the Tree! the Tree!'
short: The rediscovered tree is taken as an omen: the quest the friends shared still lives, so the poet need not despair.
body: The exclamation has an epic ring: compare the Greek soldiers' 'Thalatta! Thalatta!' ('The sea! The sea!') in Xenophon's Anabasis (4.7.24), the cry of men who have found the way home. 'I take the omen!' begins the next stanza. Though he 'cannot reach the signal-tree to-night', the tree's survival means the Gipsy-Scholar 'was not dead'. This hope is what the elegy has to offer instead of a Christian resurrection, a feature critics stress when comparing 'Thyrsis' with 'Lycidas'.

title: the Arno-vale and the 'unawakening sleep'
short: Clough lies in Florence, in the valley of the Arno, under oleanders; the 'unawakening sleep' echoes the Lament for Bion.
body: Clough is buried in the English (Protestant) Cemetery in Florence. The oleander, a Mediterranean flowering shrub, marks the southern grave against the English 'brambles pale with mist'. The phrase 'morningless and unawakening sleep' recalls the Lament for Bion, where men, unlike the garden plants, sleep a long, endless, unwakening sleep. 'Earth-forgetting eyelids' adds the idea of Lethe, oblivion. The pastoral convention would bring the mourned shepherd back to the fields; Arnold insists instead on the distance between the Italian grave and the English hills.

title: the great Mother
short: 'The great Mother' is Nature (as commentators often gloss it), with overtones of Cybele or Demeter; Thyrsis wanders in her company among the Apennines.
body: The Great Mother of antiquity was Cybele, the Phrygian goddess, often fused with Demeter or Rhea. The Phrygian setting of the next stanza (the 'Phrygian king' Lityerses) supports the link. The phrase is often glossed simply as Nature. Clough's soul now wanders in a 'boon southern country' (boon = bountiful, kindly) among the Apennines that fold round Florence. The praise in the parenthesis, 'purer or more subtle soul than thee ... the mighty Mother doth not see', is Arnold's most direct tribute.

title: Lityerses and Daphnis
short: Arnold's own note: Daphnis, ideal Sicilian shepherd, sought his love in Phrygia, where King Lityerses killed reapers he beat; Hercules saved him. The Lityerses-song was a reapers' lament.
body: Arnold's note explains that Daphnis followed his mistress Piplea to Phrygia, where King Lityerses made strangers compete with him in reaping and killed those he beat. Hercules arrived, won the contest and killed Lityerses. The 'Lityerses-song' was an ancient reapers' song. Arnold adds another tradition: Daphnis, bound by a jealous nymph's oath, loved a princess and was blinded; his father Mercury raised him to heaven, and a fountain sprang where he rose. Hence 'his blinded eyes', 'the fountain-brink' and 'the golden skies'. Daphnis's lament and death are the subject of Theocritus's first Idyll. Clough hears in the afterlife the original pastoral songs.

title: 'A fugitive and gracious light'
short: The light the Scholar seeks cannot be bought: not houses, gold, place or honour. The poet now claims the same quest, and grants it to Thyrsis too.
body: The 'light' is never defined: truth, joy, or spiritual insight beyond dogma. It is 'shy to illumine', so it shows itself rarely. The Scholar 'wends unfollow'd' and 'must house alone'. Arnold's 'and I seek it too' marks the turn from mourning to consolation. Stanza 22 extends it to Clough: 'Thou too, O Thyrsis, on like quest wast bound'. Men gave him nothing, but the quest gave him power and rest. The 'fir-topped Hurst' is Cumnor Hurst, a wooded hill.

title: 'a stormy note / Of men contention-tost'
short: Clough's later poetry of doubt and social argument (Amours de Voyage, Dipsychus) strained his 'rustic flute'; Arnold's verdict on it has been much debated.
body: Arnold says his friend's pipe lost its 'happy, country tone', 'learnt a stormy note' of men 'contention-tost', and failed: 'thou wast mute!' He means Clough's turn to the controversies of faith and society. Many modern readers think Arnold underrated Clough's ironic, experimental work (The Bothie, 1848; Amours de Voyage, 1858; the posthumous Dipsychus). They see the elegy's judgement as reflecting Arnold's own taste and his own fear for his poetic career.

title: the closing words of Thyrsis
short: The poem ends by imagining Thyrsis's own voice, in italics, coming through the city's roar: the light still shines; the tree still crowns the hill.
body: Pastoral elegies often end with a turn to consolation, as 'Lycidas' ends with the dead friend in heaven. Arnold's version is secular: an imagined whisper amid 'the great town's harsh, heart-wearying roar' (Arnold now lived in London). Thyrsis repeats the poem's symbols as proof: 'The light we sought is shining still', 'Our tree yet crowns the hill', 'Our Scholar travels yet'. The italics mark another voice, but it is Arnold's own wish speaking. That ambiguity is central to modern readings of the poem.
